verdict: OK to lend selectively in Bhiwandi powerloom — pursue integrated weavers with own processing and clean receivables; avoid pure job-work units exposed to West Asia export disruption.
title: Bhiwandi handloom & powerloom: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**A Bhiwandi powerloom unit buys yarn, weaves it into fabric on rented or owned looms, and sells to traders, garmenters or exporters.** Cash turns on loom utilisation and yarn-to-fabric conversion spread, not on brand. Value sits in the loom shed and the buyer relationship; cash sits in yarn inventory and receivables from traders. ICRA flags the sector as both fixed-capital and working-capital intensive, with funding needs typically high [8], and working capital driven by inventory holding plus receivables [9]. So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days against the trader mix; if one buyer is over a third of sales, ask for that buyer's payment history.

## What has changed now
**Local reporting says West Asia tension has slowed exports and shut a large number of powerloom units in Bhiwandi, with a relief-package demand to the Maharashtra government [3] — that source is from April 2026, so treat it as dated.** A separate AP report describes decades-old weaving businesses near Mumbai struggling to survive [2]. Against that, Maharashtra GST collections are running +8.6% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1% [D], and all-India IIP for NIC 13 (textiles) is +13.1% YoY with output +11.9% Apr-to-date [D]. Read together: the state's consumption tax base is holding, but Bhiwandi's export-facing looms are the weak spot.

## Where the growth is
**Pursue weavers with in-house processing or a direct garmenter/retail buyer, and the fabric traders who finance them.** Peer Borana Weaves shows the integrated model working: sales up 42.04% to Rs 111.36 crore in the December 2025 quarter [6], up 27.99% to Rs 100.73 crore in March 2026 [7], with a 192-machine expansion targeted at Rs 475–500 crore annual revenue and 25–30% OPM [4]. Avoid pure job-work units with no yarn ownership and single-exporter dependence — those are the ones the April report says are shutting [3].

## How to grow safely
**Structure term loans to match loom life and keep leverage low; ICRA notes low leverage preserves flexibility in a downturn [10].** Take monthly: loom utilisation, yarn purchase invoices, and a receivables ageing by buyer. Ask for GST returns each month and reconcile to sales — Maharashtra's +8.6% GST growth [D] gives you a clean cross-check. Where TUFS-type subsidy is claimed, confirm tenure against the seven-year subsidy window [10].

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for receivable days stretching past the buyer's stated terms, yarn inventory building without matching order book, and any shift from owned to job-work billing.** A unit that stops filing GST or shows sales falling while IIP textiles is +13.1% [D] is losing share, not riding a cycle. Note the bank credit-to-output gap of +3.3 pp [D]: system credit is outrunning output, so some of what you see is leverage, not demand.
